analysis.one_liner: Requires new keyless-ignition cars to shut off automatically and resist rolling away.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee from June 2019 until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation to finish safety rules for cars with keyless (push-button) ignitions. Carmakers would have to install technology that shuts the engine off automatically after it idles long enough to risk carbon monoxide building up, and technology that stops a car from rolling away when the driver's door is open, the seat belt is unbuckled, the brake is off, and the car is not in park. The rules would have taken effect about a year after they were issued.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, passengers, and people near parked cars. Every year drivers have died of carbon monoxide poisoning after leaving a keyless-ignition car running in a closed garage, and children and others have been hurt or killed when cars left in gear rolled away. The bill would have made those failure modes much harder by requiring the car itself to shut off or lock in place.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers, families, and people near parked cars

how_it_helps.text: Requires every new car with a keyless ignition and a gas engine to shut off automatically after idling for a period set by safety regulators to prevent carbon monoxide poisoning.

Requires new keyless-ignition cars with automatic transmissions to include technology that prevents the car from rolling away when the door is open, the seat belt is unbuckled, the brake is off, and the car is not in park.
Sets firm deadlines: the Department of Transportation must issue final rules within two years of enactment, and each rule takes effect the following September 1.
The sponsor introduced it with three other members, and the bill drew cosponsors from both parties.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers, who would bear the cost of designing, testing, and installing the shutoff and rollaway-prevention technology, and who would likely pass some of that cost into new-car prices. The Department of Transportation would take on the work of completing the rulemakings.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on automakers and ultimately on car buyers, including buyers who would never leave a car idling or in gear; those costs are spread across every new vehicle sold rather than only on the riskiest ones.

The bill tells regulators exactly what to require and on what schedule, which leaves less room for the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to weigh feasibility, alternative designs, or differing emission rates across vehicle types (though it does allow different shutoff periods for different vehicle types).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefit is targeted and real: automatic shutoff addresses documented carbon monoxide deaths from keyless cars left running indoors, and rollaway prevention addresses a well-known failure mode involving children and unattended vehicles. The cost is modest per vehicle and spread across all buyers. The main design critique is that Congress dictated the rule's content and deadline rather than leaving the details to the safety agency. On balance the benefit outweighs the cost for the people the rules protect.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its consumer protection subcommittee, and neither ever held a hearing or vote, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Janice Schakowsky introduced the PARK IT Act on June 5, 2019, with Representatives Soto, Moulton, and Kennedy as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce.
The bill attracted 10 cosponsors, 6 Democrats and 4 Republicans.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in the House, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers are better off: no mandatory shutoff or rollaway-prevention technology was required of them, and the existing voluntary level of compliance continued. Drivers exposed to carbon monoxide and rollaway risks gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Automakers, who faced no new mandate

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on June 6, 2019 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded, but the bill's initial support was bipartisan: of its 11 supporters, 6 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and 4 were Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have required them to design and install automatic shutoff and rollaway-prevention technology on all new keyless-ignition cars within a few years, adding engineering and per-vehicle costs. In this bill the industry's cost is the public's safety gain, so its interest runs against ordinary people's on the specific requirement, though major automakers already comply with some related regulations.

Buyers would receive safer vehicles but would likely pay slightly more per new car because compliance costs are spread across the fleet. Buyers of used cars and vehicles over 10,000 pounds, motorcycles, and trailers are excluded from the mandate.
